title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Mozart and the ABCs
hook: Twinkle, Twinkle, the alphabet song and Baa, Baa share one French tune.
peek: Sing Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star, then the ABC song, then Baa, Baa, Black Sheep. They are the same melody, an 18th-century French tune. Mozart wrote famous variations on it, but he did not compose it.
lede: Three of the first songs many English-speaking children learn use one melody. It began as a French song, Ah vous dirai-je, maman, which first appeared in print in 1761. Its simple shape, a leap up, a step higher, then gently down, made it easy to fit to new words. People often credit Mozart with the tune, but he only borrowed it.

bullets.text: The French title means oh, shall I tell you, mother. The earliest known words are a young woman's confession to her mother that she has fallen in love, and the tune spread quickly across Europe as a popular air.
Around 1781 or 1782, Mozart wrote twelve piano variations on the melody. They dress the simple tune in runs, a minor-key turn and flourishes, and are a favourite of piano students.
The words of Twinkle, Twinkle come from a poem by the English writer Jane Taylor, published in 1806. Only later was it paired with the French melody.

The alphabet song was copyrighted in Boston in 1835 by the publisher Charles Bradlee, who described the tune as a German air. Fitting 26 letters into the melody is why L, M, N, O and P famously blur together.
